name: Freya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting me in, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a construction crew at the Garrow depot, in the old coal valley. The pits shut long ago, and now the company's building lines to hook up the wind turbines on the hills and the solar panels on the old pit land. So my days are digging pole holes, setting new poles, stringing new wire, a lot of mud and a lot of hard hats.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building something new in a valley that's been knocked down for thirty years. I use AI every day, on the job to read the specs faster and at night to price up jobs for the little home repair business Mark and I run on weekends. What wears me out is the money; Garrow pays below the city, Mark's carpentry dried up last winter and it ate what we'd saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd almost be disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, more poles for us to plant. With friends I'd say the useful bits are useful, and I'd keep using them. Online I'd probably post a little rant about the people who said it would save the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down, because I was hoping the tools would keep getting better for our little business. But I'm fine. The wind farms still need connecting, so there's work for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep using AI to price jobs and do our books. I'd push the weekend business harder, maybe get the kitchen-fitting side going properly with Mark. And I'd put any extra into rebuilding the savings we lost last winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does AI help with the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take photos of a job, tell it the measurements, and it gives me a list of materials and a rough price. Then I check it against what the builder's merchant charges. Last month it saved us from under-quoting a bathroom by about four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you lose last winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two months of savings, all of it really. Mark had six weeks with nothing, and we kept the mortgage paid by living on soup and my overtime. I swore we'd never be that close again.

S0.say: She'd say good, more poles for the crew to plant, and that the useful bits are useful. Online she'd post a little rant about people who said AI would save the world.
S0.think: Privately she'd be a bit let down because she hoped the tools would keep improving for her small business. But she's fine, with years of wind farm connections still to build.
S0.do: Keeps doing her job and using AI for quoting and bookkeeping. Pushes the weekend business into kitchen fitting with her husband and puts any extra into rebuilding lost savings.
S0.quote: Last month it saved us from under-quoting a bathroom by about four hundred.
S0.fieldNote: Freya thinks like a small business owner as much as a lineworker. The winter that wiped out their savings is a recent, sharp memory. She sees AI mostly as a practical tool for making money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that sounds about right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say get stuck in, learn the new kit, nobody owes us a living. With friends I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work. I'd share stuff about small businesses using the tools well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The line work stays because someone has to build all these wind connections. And our weekend business gets sharper with better tools, so we could grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new planning software comes to the depot, first in line. I'd use AI to get our weekend business online properly, with a website and booking. And I'd look at buying a small second-hand digger for the weekend jobs, on finance, if the numbers worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A digger on finance after losing all your savings. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But a digger earns money, the savings account doesn't. I'd only do it if I had three months of bookings lined up. My dad would say I'm reckless, but he also says I'm the only one in the family who's ever started anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Brian. He's a good man, but he won't even use the text messages for the rota. I'd sit with him in the van and show him. You don't leave your own behind.

S1.say: She'd tell colleagues to get stuck in and learn the new kit because nobody owes them a living. With friends she'd call it a chance for people willing to work.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her: wind connections keep line work going, and better tools sharpen the weekend business enough to grow it.
S1.do: Learns the new depot planning software first in line and uses AI to put the weekend business online with a website and booking. Considers a second-hand digger on finance if three months of bookings are lined up.
S1.quote: A digger earns money, the savings account doesn't.
S1.fieldNote: Her appetite for risk is clear even after a bruising winter. Her free-market view sits alongside a strong duty to colleagues like Brian. She wants the business to grow, not just survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's a jolt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say adapt or get flattened, and help each other through. At church I'd say families and neighbours have to look after each other, because the government won't move fast enough. Online I'd be posting about how small businesses can use the robots instead of being crushed by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd say. If robots can build lines and fit kitchens, both my jobs and Mark's are gone. The only way through I can see is to be the people who set the robots up for everyone else, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the weekend business into a robot set-up business for local farms, builders and households, in the first six months. I'd cut everything at home that doesn't earn money. And I'd keep my depot job as long as they'd have me, because that's the steady wage while the business finds its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which feels wrong to say. But scared about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both jobs gone. How long could you last without either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three weeks. That's the honest number. Which is why I'd be moving fast, not because I'm brave but because I can't afford to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella and Jack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Mum and Dad are starting a new business and they might have to help. Ella's fourteen, she's better with this stuff than me, so I'd actually put her to work on the website. It'd be good for her.

S2.say: She'd tell colleagues to adapt or get flattened and help each other through, and tell her church that neighbours must look after each other because government won't move fast enough. Online she'd post about small businesses using robots.
S2.think: Privately it worries her more than she'd admit: robots building lines and fitting kitchens would take both her and her husband's work. Her only way through is becoming the people who set robots up for others, fast.
S2.do: Turns the weekend business into a robot set-up service for local farms, builders and households within six months. Cuts all spending that doesn't earn money and keeps her depot job as a steady wage while the business grows.
S2.feel: Anxious and oddly excited, but scared about the mortgage.
S2.quote: Not because I'm brave but because I can't afford to stand still.
S2.fieldNote: Her speed comes from necessity, not just temperament, and she says so plainly. She'd turn the threat into a business idea immediately. Faith and community are her safety net rather than government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I can build something in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got time to get ready, so don't waste it moaning. With friends I'd say this is the best chance in a generation for people to start their own thing. At church I'd say look after the folk who can't change as fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build a proper business. I'd be setting up robots for others before most people have even started thinking. Mark would come in full-time by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the robot set-up service alongside the depot job, using AI to learn the systems at night. I'd put every penny of profit back into a van and tools. By year three I'd hand in my notice at the depot if the business was paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. The good kind of nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hand in your notice with thin savings. What would make you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of the business paying the mortgage on its own, and a few months in the bank. I'm not daft. I'd want proof before I jump, but I'd jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the only way through was to set up robots. Doesn't the AI eventually set itself up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Then I'd need to move again, maybe into teaching people, or something else. I don't think anything lasts forever, that's why you keep moving.

S3.say: She'd tell colleagues there's time to get ready, so don't waste it moaning, and call it the best chance in a generation to start your own thing. At church she'd ask people to look after those who can't change as fast.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to build a proper business setting up robots for others, with her husband joining full-time by year two.
S3.do: Starts the robot set-up service alongside the depot job in year one, learning systems at night with AI. Reinvests profit in a van and tools and leaves the depot by year three once the business has paid the mortgage for six months.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, the good kind of nerves.
S3.quote: I'm not daft. I'd want proof before I jump, but I'd jump.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her into a full planner with clear tests for leaving her job. She accepts that the robot business won't last forever and expects to keep moving. Her concern for slower colleagues sits alongside her drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nobody can complain they weren't warned. I'd tell the young ones to save, learn and start something. At church I'd say families should plan together, because that's what families are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is mostly good for me. I'd build the business slowly, rebuild our savings, and get the kids through school. My worry is more for the valley, because it's already been knocked down once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend business steadily over the first few years, using AI for everything from quotes to accounts. I'd talk to Ella and Jack about what they want to do, maybe bring them into the business. And I'd keep my depot job until the business was clearly safe, probably year four or five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I like having a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry for the valley. What would you want for Garrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small businesses starting here, run by people from here. The pits taught us what happens when one big employer leaves. I'd rather twenty small ones than one big one again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Ella and Jack in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they want it. I'd want them to know how to run something, even if they end up doing something else. Knowing how to make your own work is the best thing I can give them.

S4.say: She'd say nobody can complain they weren't warned and tell young colleagues to save, learn and start something. At church she'd say families should plan together.
S4.think: Privately ten years is mostly good for her: time to build the business slowly, rebuild savings and get the kids through school. Her worry is for the valley, which has been knocked down once already.
S4.do: Grows the weekend business steadily, using AI for quotes and accounts, and keeps the depot job until the business is clearly safe around year four or five. Talks with her children about joining the business.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, liking the long runway.
S4.quote: I'd rather twenty small ones than one big one again.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she becomes calm and almost cheerful about the future. The pit closures shape her preference for many small local firms. She sees teaching her children to make their own work as her main legacy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because with three weeks of money there's no room to build anything properly. What would help is easy small business loans for people starting out, not handouts, and the company giving us notice so we can plan. And cheap training on the new systems, evenings, for people with jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me are already doing. Half the crew has something on the side. We're not waiting for anyone to save us, we just need a fair chance to get going.

headlineQuote: We're not waiting for anyone to save us, we just need a fair chance to get going.
portrait: Freya Petrov is a 43-year-old construction lineworker connecting wind and solar farms in an old coal valley, with a carpenter husband, two kids and savings wiped out by a lean winter. She uses AI every day, at work and for the weekend home repair business she runs with her husband. She'd be slightly disappointed by a plateau and excited by steady change. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious and pushes her straight into a robot set-up business out of necessity, while five and ten years let her build it carefully before leaving the depot. She believes in small businesses, family and church, and wants many small local firms for her valley.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with about three weeks of money there'd be no room to build anything properly.
whatWouldHelp: Easy small business loans rather than handouts, early notice from the company, and cheap evening training on new systems.
